steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a survey of confidence estimation and calibration in large language models. Motivate why trustworthiness matters, explain why existing methods are hard to apply to LLMs, and describe the survey's scope and structure.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. LLM capabilities and their reliability problems
2. Confidence estimation and calibration: background
3. Challenges of applying these methods to LLMs
4. Gap in existing surveys; our scope and structure

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. LLM capabilities and problems
- capabilities: world knowledge storage, sophisticated language-based reasoning, in-context learning
- not consistently good performance
- biases, hallucinations not aligned with reality
- evaluating trustworthiness of responses still challenging

2. Background
- confidence (uncertainty) estimation crucial for out-of-distribution detection, selective prediction
- extensively studied and applied in various contexts
- model calibration: align predictive probabilities (estimated confidence) with actual accuracy

3. Challenges for LLMs
- output space much larger than discriminative models
- possible outcomes grow exponentially with generation length -> can't access all responses
- different expressions, same meaning -> consider semantics
- unique properties: expressing confidence in words; zero-shot / few-shot learning
- prompt sensitivity (examples and their order) -> instability
- so confidence estimation and calibration for LLMs = emerging area of interest

4. Our survey
- existing surveys: hallucination, factuality
- no comprehensive survey systematically discussing technical advancements -> bridge gap
- unique challenges, latest studies
- Section 2: confidence, uncertainty, calibration for neural models
- Section 3: generation tasks; Section 4: classification tasks
- Section 5: practical applications; Section 6: future directions
- Figure 1: survey structure
- goal: illuminate this facet, more reliable applications

steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) have shown a wide range of capabilities, for example storing world knowledge, sophisticated language-based reasoning, and in-context learning. But LLMs do not always achieve good performance. What they generate still has biases and hallucinations that do not match reality. It is still challenging to evaluate how trustworthy the responses from these models are.

Confidence (or uncertainty) estimation is crucial for tasks like out-of-distribution detection and selective prediction, and it has been studied and applied a lot in various contexts. A related concept is model calibration, which is about aligning the predictive probabilities (the estimated confidence) with the actual accuracy.

- output space much larger than discriminative models; outcomes grow exponentially with length
- same meaning, different expressions -> semantics
- confidence in words; zero-shot / few-shot learning
- prompt sensitivity (examples, order) -> instability
- emerging area of interest

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) have shown a wide range of capabilities, for example storing world knowledge, sophisticated language-based reasoning, and in-context learning. But LLMs do not always achieve good performance. What they generate still has biases and hallucinations that do not match reality. It is still challenging to evaluate how trustworthy the responses from these models are.

Confidence (or uncertainty) estimation is crucial for tasks like out-of-distribution detection and selective prediction, and it has been studied and applied a lot in various contexts. A related concept is model calibration, which is about aligning the predictive probabilities (the estimated confidence) with the actual accuracy.

But there are several challenges when these methods are applied directly to LLMs. The output space of these models is much larger than that of discriminative models. The number of possible outcomes grows exponentially with the length of the generation, so it is impossible to access all the potential responses. Also, different expressions can convey the same meaning, which suggests confidence estimation should take semantics into account. Finally, LLMs have unique properties, like expressing confidence in words and being able to do zero-shot or few-shot learning. Still, their responses can be sensitive to the prompts, e.g., which examples are provided and in what order, and this can make the results very unstable. Because of all this, confidence estimation and calibration for LLMs is growing as an emerging area of interest.

Existing surveys mainly focused on issues like hallucination and factuality in LLMs, and there is no comprehensive survey that systematically discusses the technical advancements in LLMs, so here we want to bridge this gap. We look at the unique challenges that LLMs pose and examine the latest studies that address them. First we discuss key concepts like confidence, uncertainty, and calibration in the context of neural models, in Section 2. Then we go in two different directions: confidence estimation and calibration techniques for generation tasks in Section 3, and for classification tasks in Section 4. At the end we explore their practical applications (Section 5) and look at potential future research directions (Section 6). Figure 1 gives a comprehensive representation of how the survey is structured. With a detailed examination of the existing research, our goal is to shed light on this vital facet of LLMs and contribute to developing more reliable applications.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated a wide range of capabilities, such as storing world knowledge, sophisticated language-based reasoning, and in-context learning [1,2,3]. However, LLMs do not consistently achieve good performance [4,5]. Their generations still include biases [6,7] and hallucinations that do not align with reality [5]. Evaluating the trustworthiness of responses from these models remains challenging [8].

Confidence (or uncertainty) estimation is crucial for tasks like out-of-distribution detection and selective prediction [9,10], and it has been extensively studied and applied in various contexts [11,12]. A related concept is model calibration, which focuses on aligning predictive probabilities (estimated confidence) with actual accuracy [13].

However, applying these methods directly to LLMs presents several challenges. The output space of these models is significantly larger than that of discriminative models, and the number of possible outcomes grows exponentially with the generation length, making it impossible to access all potential responses. In addition, different expressions may convey the same meaning, suggesting that confidence estimation should take semantics into account. Lastly, LLMs show unique properties, such as expressing confidence in words [14,15] and the ability to perform zero-shot or few-shot learning [3]. Nonetheless, their responses can be sensitive to the prompts, e.g., the examples provided and their order, which can cause considerable instability in the results. Given this, confidence estimation and calibration for LLMs is growing as an emerging area of interest [16,14,17,18].

While existing surveys have mainly focused on issues such as hallucination and factuality in LLMs [5,19], no comprehensive survey systematically discusses the technical advancements in LLMs, and we aim to bridge this gap. We explore the unique challenges posed by LLMs and examine the latest studies that address them. We first discuss key concepts such as confidence, uncertainty, and calibration in the context of neural models in Section 2. We then pursue two directions: confidence estimation and calibration techniques for generation tasks in Section 3, and for classification tasks in Section 4. We conclude by exploring their practical applications (Section 5) and potential future research directions (Section 6). Figure 1 provides a comprehensive representation of the survey's structure. Through a detailed examination of existing research, our goal is to illuminate this vital facet of LLMs and contribute to the development of more reliable applications.
